conceptTag: A restaurant group with $1M of profit
readerTitle: A restaurant group made $1M. Where should it go?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (4개 매장 레스토랑 그룹, 냉난방 설비 서비스 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 이익을 어디에 쓸지는 아이디어의 매력이 아니라 1달러당 수익률 순서와 넘어야 할 기준선으로 정한다.
misconception: 잘되는 매장이 있으면 같은 매장을 하나 더 여는 것이 이익을 쓰는 가장 당연한 방법이다.

factChecks.note: 설명 단순화를 위해 세금, 감가상각, 신규 매장의 초기 적자 기간을 수익률 계산에서 뺐습니다. 카드 7에서 예측 낙관 편향을 한계로 언급합니다.

cards.title: A restaurant group made $1M. Where should it go?
body: Maria runs four busy restaurants. This year the group made **$1M in profit**, and the cash is sitting in the bank.
Her chef wants a fifth location. Her partner wants to buy a rival. Her banker mentions the loan. Everyone has a good idea. Only one pot of money.

image.label: A bag of cash on a restaurant table surrounded by four ideas
image.brief: 레스토랑 테이블 위에 돈 자루 하나. 주변에 네 개의 말풍선: 새 매장 건물, 테라스, 다른 식당 간판, 대출 서류. 따뜻한 조명의 일러스트. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where do the first dollars go?
body: The options: a fifth restaurant ($1M, about $150k a year once running), buying a rival's two restaurants ($1M, about $120k a year), or a covered patio at the flagship ($200k, about $60k a year more profit).

options.text: The fifth restaurant. It copies what already works
options.feedback: It feels safe because the concept is proven. But it earns 15% on each dollar, half what the patio earns.

options.text: The patio first, then judge the rest
options.feedback: The patio returns 30% a year on its cost, the highest **return on invested capital** on the table. Fund the best return per dollar first.

options.text: Buy the rival. It adds two restaurants at once
options.feedback: You gain size fast but earn only 12% on the money, the lowest of the three. Bigger is not the same as better use of cash.

cards.title: Each option, per dollar invested.
body: Same $1M of profit, very different results. The patio is small, but every dollar works twice as hard as a dollar in a new restaurant.

cards.title: Return on invested capital sets the order.
body: **Return on invested capital** is the yearly profit a project adds, divided by the money it takes. It lets you compare a patio with a whole restaurant on the same scale.
Sorted this way, the patio goes first. The new restaurant would earn less than Maria's current ones do. That doesn't kill it, but it means growth would *lower* her group's average return.

image.label: Four bars ranked by return per dollar
image.brief: 가로 막대 4개를 수익률 순으로 정렬: Patio 30%, Existing 25%, New site 15%, Buy rival 12%. 맨 위 막대만 강조 색. 깔끔한 인포그래픽.

cards.title: A hurdle rate decides what's left.
body: After the patio, $800k remains. Maria sets a **hurdle rate**: the minimum return a risky project must beat to get money. Restaurants fail often, so she picks 15%.
The rival at 12% falls short. The new site sits right on the line. And there's a safe option: paying off her 8% loan saves $64k of interest a year, with no risk at all.

cards.title: What happens to the other $800k?
body: The fifth restaurant is forecast at exactly 15%, her hurdle rate. What should Maria do?

options.text: Build it. It meets the hurdle
options.feedback: On paper, yes. But a project that only *just* clears the **hurdle rate** has no room for a slow first year or a cost overrun.

options.text: Pay down the loan and keep looking for projects that clear the bar easily
options.feedback: A certain 8% beats a risky 15% that could easily become 10%. The **hurdle rate** works best when it leaves a safety margin.

options.text: Buy the rival. It's cheaper than building from scratch
options.feedback: Cheaper to start, but 12% is below the **hurdle rate**. You'd take on restaurant risk for less than the bar you set.

cards.title: The returns are guesses.
body: Every number here is a forecast. New locations often take a year or two to reach their expected profit, and owners tend to love their own plans.
High-return projects are also usually small. The patio can only absorb $200k. Don't stretch a great small idea into a big mediocre one.
And never count repairs to existing kitchens as optional. Keeping what works running comes before any new bet.

cards.title: Now it's a heating and cooling company.
body: Sam's repair company made $300k. His hurdle rate is 20%. Options: a second van and technician ($90k, adds $40k a year after wages), scheduling software ($60k, adds $15k a year), or a showroom ($250k, adds $20k a year).

options.text: The showroom. It makes the business look established
options.feedback: It may impress customers, but 8% is far below the 20% **hurdle rate**. It uses the most cash for the least return.

options.text: The van first, then the software
options.feedback: The van returns about 44% and the software 25%. Both clear the **hurdle rate**, and ranking by **return on invested capital** puts the van first.

options.text: Only the software. Digital tools scale best
options.feedback: It clears the bar at 25%, but it skips the van, which earns almost twice as much per dollar.

cards.softwareNote: A software company does the same math: one more engineer, a new market, or paying down debt. Rank each by yearly profit per dollar and drop anything below the bar.

cards.title: Rank by return, then hold the line.
body: Maria used two ideas. **Return on invested capital** set the order: patio first. A **hurdle rate** decided the rest: no project below the bar, and a safe loan payoff over a risky maybe.
**Try it today:** list three things you could spend your next profit on. Write the cost and the yearly profit each would add, then divide.
